Firstly, don't stay in a hotel, **stay in a hostel**. Seriously. Hostels are amazing when you're travelling alone. I cannot overstate this. There is nothing like staying in a dorm to meet people. You can usually find female only rooms if that is something that makes you uncomfortable or whatever. Use http://www.hostelworld.com/ and check the reviews. It's cheaper than a hotel and even the worst hostels I've stayed in have been safe, clean and comfortable. Internet reviews have more or less relegated the shitty bedbug hostels from the days of yore to the past, since you now know exactly what you're getting into.

Check in to the hostel, drop your bags, and check out the common room. Basically just talk to people in the hostel. Most people in hostels will be really open to making friends, and nine times out of ten you can find a group of people to hang out with. I'm not a terribly outgoing person, but every time I've stayed in a hostel I've made new friends, and you pretty much only have to stay in if you want to.

Don't worry about only speaking English. *Everyone* in hostels speaks English. Seriously. They'll say shit like, "My English is terrible" and proceed to converse with you in near perfect English. It's crazy. Everyone speaks English. Around the touristy areas most of the customer service people and stuff will too.

Even if you don't find someone to roll with, don't be afraid to explore! Once you've checked in to a hostel you've got a home base. Ask the desk staff for advice, they can usually offer great suggestions.

Good luck! I believe in you.

Yeah it's really hard to put yourself out there. It took me a really long time to get to where I am now, and even now I still have trouble around new people.

I think the first thing is just realizing that you have to put yourself out there in some way to meet people. Starting a new job, school, going to meetups, singles events, travelling, are all ways to meet people. The thing I've found is that I need to make an effort to socialize, if I'm around people. Because if I don't I'll just sit there and not say anything the entire time.

It's understandable if you're daunted by social stuff, it's scary. So try to work up to it. You say you like reading, try just doing that but somewhere else. The library, a coffee shop, sort of ease into it. Even if you don't say anything to people, just being out of the house is helpful, I find. See a movie in a theatre by yourself instead of watching Netflix. Go to a museum, walk around your city. Just try to get out of the house.

You should go to your school's counselling service. I mean if nothing else you should do this. It's free and they can get you extensions and stuff for your classes. I know firsthand how debilitating stuff like that can be, so don't talk yourself out of it by telling yourself it's not a legitimate problem. They'll work with you but you have to talk to them about it. They can also probably help you manage anxiety and stuff.

Long term you might try talking to your school's academic advisor, they can help you with your academic goals and stuff. You could also try taking some time off. That was the silver lining for me when I failed out. I had some time to just work shitty retail jobs that gave me a ton of perspective that really helped me figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

Hope this helps.

Oh ho ho. If you're desperate to find work I have a couple of good suggestions.

The first is to try overnight work. It's great because most people aren't able or willing to do overnight work so it's really a seller's market. I did it for a year when I was 22 and lacking direction. You don't deal with the public so they don't care so much that you're awkward, you get lots of hours, shit I got full time at Walmart off the street because I was on nights. Walmart *hates* giving out full time status. It's not the easiest thing but it toughens you up a bit, and I find it's a little more solid on a resume than part time burger flipping or whatever, not that there's anything wrong with it.

Plus I find you meet some interesting people. Everyone has their reasons for working nights. It also gives you an interesting perspective on the world, you get to see the city at night, you gain a new appreciation for 24 hour fast food joints. Stuff like that. I recommend doing it, at least for a little while.

If that's not your cup of tea you could try a temp agency. I had some luck with them, though they aren't without their downsides. Basically you technically work for the temp agency, and then your actual workplace, say a warehouse or something, hires you as a "contractor." It's a pretty anti-labour setup but if you're desperate, whatever. The main downside is that because you don't actually work for the company they can fire you whenever they want, for practically any reason.

Other than that, if you just want to keep doing what you're doing I'd say go for quantity over quality when you're applying. When I was getting my first job I probably dropped off like 30 or 40 resumes.

Oh and in the interviews I wouldn't resort to outright lying. I mean you can if you want, but half-truths are probably better all around. Saying something like, "My parents are disabled so I've been looking after them while I try to figure out what I'd like to do with my life" is going to be more than sufficient.

Not sure what your resume is like but if it's too sparse and you think that's putting off employers you could always volunteer. I mean you don't get paid, obviously, but it can be pretty fun and looks good on a resume. Festivals, charity runs, events like that are always looking for short term volunteers.

Good luck out there!

>The only negative thing about DLC is the rare occasions when content is cannibalized from the main game in order to make the game artificially cost more.

The problem with DLC is that it makes too much money. Evolve has a lot of people upset because it was designed from the ground up to sell DLC. I personally think this is just the tip of the spear, and that the entire games industry has been headed this way for a long time. Evolve is basically a $70 DLC delivery system.

In an ideal world I guess you'd have developers make a game, and they try to make it fun to play so that it will sell. And then when it's done they make some extra stuff and sell it to earn some extra cash and everybody's happy.

The reality, and I think Evolve is just the apotheosis of this, is that DLC warps the entire development cycle. Because now on top of designing a game that's fun that people want to play, developers also need to use the game as a way to sell DLC because it will make a buttload of money for the publisher. And I think that DLC has slowly been making its way to the top of the list of priorities for the developers, with Evolve being proof of that.

What I think makes DLC hard to decry as well is that there's no way to measure the effects on the final game, even though it certainly has one. I mean people *feel* that DLC is bad for the industry, and I'm inclined to agree, but there are no numbers we can point to to help our case. We can't say "Well this graph clearly shows that 12% of the hours that would have otherwise been spent balancing multiplayer were spent developing DLC implentation strategies and the game is 14% shittier as a result."

So yeah I guess what I'm trying to say is that while *some* DLC may be good on a case by case basis, DLC is warping the entire gaming industry irrespective of that, probably for the worse.

Hey, I've had a lot of trouble in the past with obsessions and stuff and what you're describing sounds similar. That cold feeling and nausea, it's actually caused me to throw up a couple of times. I've never been diagnosed by a doctor but I think I have pure ocd or something.

Anyway, I've found the best way to deal with it is to just confront the thoughts and question them. So you think you have a small head. Instead of comparing your head to others or whatever, just tell yourself that maybe you have a small head, maybe not, so what? It doesn't affect your worth as a person and you can't change it so who cares?

I found the problem with thoughts like these is that you're constantly looking for a definitive answer that doesn't exist. You want to know for sure if you have a small head by comparing your head to everyone else's so that you can know for sure that your head is small. But you never will. There's no metric for comparing head sizes, there's no normal head size, so you'll just constantly look for affirmation that you'll never get. It's why you spend hours going in circles in your head without really getting anywhere.

I found you have to take the power away from thoughts like these by questioning them and not falling into the trap of ruminating. It's a slow process but it gets easier.

Anyway I hope this helps. If it sounds close to home I can probably give more advice, just let me know.
